title: The 'Carbon Copy' Film That Pakistan Banned: The Story of Bedari and Jagriti
excerpt: Pakistan's 1957 patriotic hit Bedari was a scene-for-scene copy of India's Jagriti — and once audiences realised, the ban triggered an uproar.
body:
• Pakistan's 1957 Urdu film Bedari was a scene-for-scene copy of India's 1954 patriotic classic Jagriti — down to the patriotic anthem, with the word "Pakistan" swapped in for "Hindustan."
  • Released on December 6, 1957, Bedari became one of the biggest hits of the year in Pakistan before audiences realised what they were watching.
  • Once the copying was exposed, Pakistan banned the film, triggering an uproar among fans of what had been one of the country's most beloved patriotic films.
  • The episode, revisited in a new Indian Express retrospective, remains one of cinema's strangest cross-border plagiarism cases.

It was one of the most patriotic films Pakistan ever produced — and it wasn't Pakistani at all. In 1957, the Urdu-language film Bedari stormed Pakistani cinemas, its songs on every tongue and its box-office run among the year's biggest. Then audiences realised they had seen it all before: Bedari was a carbon copy of India's Jagriti, right down to the anthem.

According to the Indian Express retrospective that has revived the story, the copying was brazen even by the standards of an era when plagiarism in South Asian cinema was common. Bedari reproduced Jagriti's story scene for scene — and lifted its patriotic song wholesale, simply inserting the word "Pakistan" where the original said "Hindustan."

A copy too perfect

Bedari, a black-and-white Urdu melodrama, was released on December 6, 1957, and proved to be one of the greatest hits of the year in Pakistan. It became one of the most patriotic Pakistani films ever made, and its songs are still remembered today — an irony that deepens with time, given that the music, the story and even the nationalist fervour were imported across the border.

Jagriti, the 1954 Indian original, was itself a landmark of patriotic cinema, a film that defined how a generation of Indians imagined nationhood on screen. That its doppelganger could pass unnoticed for months speaks to how completely the two countries' film cultures still overlapped a decade after Partition — the same melodies, the same storytelling grammar, the same audience.

The ban and the uproar

The spell broke when Pakistani audiences began to recognise the film they were cheering. Once the word spread that Bedari was Jagriti in disguise, the authorities banned it — and the ban, rather than settling the matter, caused a mass uproar among viewers who had made the film a phenomenon.

The incident fits a longer pattern of cinema getting caught in the crossfire of India-Pakistan relations. In 2017, Pakistan's Sindh Film Censor Board banned Gurinder Chadha's Partition: 1947, the Hindi version of Viceroy's House, over what it called the misrepresentation of Muhammad Ali Jinnah.

"We felt his character was not portrayed correctly and it felt strange. Although the character only appears in a few scenes... the actor didn't look like Jinnah at all."

— Abdul Razzaq Khuhawar, secretary, Sindh Film Censor Board, on Partition: 1947

Blanket bans have followed each spike in tensions — after the 2016 Uri attack, after the 2019 Balakot strikes, and after the revocation of Article 370 — with Pakistani exhibitors repeatedly announcing boycotts of Indian films, and Indian industry bodies responding in kind.

Why the story endures

What makes Bedari different from the routine bans is the direction of the copying. This was not a government censoring a neighbour's film; it was a Pakistani studio building a nationalist classic out of an Indian one, and a Pakistani public embracing it before the secret came out. The episode remains a favourite anecdote for film historians because it captures something real about the subcontinent's shared cinema: the melodies and stories flowed across the border even when little else did.

For the diaspora, raised on both countries' film music and often nostalgic for the pre-Partition cultural world, the Bedari saga is a reminder of how deeply intertwined the two industries once were — and how strange the attempts to disentangle them have been.
